title: Psychology: How Minds Work
description: Detect a faint signal, watch a memory fade and recover, and test the classic studies against their replications.
audience: An adult comfortable with percentages, square roots and simple algebra. No previous psychology or statistics course is assumed.

sources.title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: 97 of 100 original studies reported significant results; 35 of the 97 replications (36%) were significant, and mean effect sizes roughly halved. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Open Science Collaboration (2015), Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science, Science 349(6251), aac4716.

sources.title: A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: 23 laboratories and 2,141 participants; pooled effect d = 0.04, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.15, against d = 0.62 in the 2010 meta-analysis of published studies that motivated it. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Hagger, Chatzisarantis and 47 co-authors (2016), A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect, Perspectives on Psychological Science 11(4), 546–573.

sources.title: Assessing the robustness of power posing
sources.publisher: Ranehill, Dreber, Johannesson, Leiberg, Sul and Weber (2015)
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: With 200 participants, power poses did not change testosterone, cortisol or risk taking. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Ranehill, Dreber, Johannesson, Leiberg, Sul and Weber (2015), Assessing the robustness of power posing, Psychological Science 26(5), 653–656.

sources.title: Behavioral priming: it's all in the mind, but whose mind?
sources.licence: Creative Commons Attribution License, as stated on the PLOS ONE article; used for fact checking only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Infrared-timed walking speed was not slowed by elderly-related words; slowing appeared only when experimenters expected it. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Doyen, Klein, Pichon and Cleeremans (2012), Behavioral priming: it's all in the mind, but whose mind?, PLoS ONE 7(1), e29081.

sources.title: Sixteen S-squared over D-squared: a relation for crude sample size estimates
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: About 16/d² participants per group give 80% power for a two-sided test at α = 0.05. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Lehr (1992), Sixteen S-squared over D-squared: a relation for crude sample size estimates, Statistics in Medicine 11(8), 1099–1102.

sources.title: Gorillas in our midst: sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Across conditions, 46% of observers counting passes failed to notice an unexpected person walking through the game. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Simons and Chabris (1999), Gorillas in our midst: sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events, Perception 28(9), 1059–1074.

sources.title: Task switching
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Switching between tasks lengthens responses compared with repeating a task; preparation reduces but does not remove the cost. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Monsell (2003), Task switching, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 7(3), 134–140.

sources.title: Supertaskers: profile and analysis of extraordinary multitasking ability
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Of 200 participants driving a simulator while doing a demanding verbal task, 5 (2.5%) showed no dual-task cost. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Watson and Strayer (2010), Supertaskers: profile and analysis of extraordinary multitasking ability, Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 17(4), 479–485.

sources.title: Humans integrate visual and haptic information in a statistically optimal fashion
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Visual and touch estimates of height are combined with weights close to their relative reliabilities. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Ernst and Banks (2002), Humans integrate visual and haptic information in a statistically optimal fashion, Nature 415, 429–433.

sources.title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: When rehearsal and chunking are controlled, adults hold about three to five chunks. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Cowan (2001), The magical number 4 in short-term memory, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(1), 87–114.

sources.title: Perception in chess
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: A master recalled real game positions far better than weaker players, grouping pieces into meaningful chunks; the advantage vanished for randomly placed pieces. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Chase and Simon (1973), Perception in chess, Cognitive Psychology 4(1), 55–81.

sources.title: Short-term memory for word sequences as a function of acoustic, semantic and formal similarity
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Immediate serial recall is much poorer for lists of similar-sounding words than for dissimilar words, while similarity of meaning matters little. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Baddeley (1966), Short-term memory for word sequences as a function of acoustic, semantic and formal similarity, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology 18(4), 362–365.

sources.title: Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve
sources.licence: Creative Commons Attribution License, as stated on the PLOS ONE article; used for fact checking only
sources.notes: Checked figure: A single-participant replication of Ebbinghaus's savings method reproduced his steep early loss and slower later decline, with savings of 0.58 after 20 minutes and 0.44 after an hour, and a bump above the fitted curve at one day. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Murre and Dros (2015), Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve, PLoS ONE 10(7), e0120644.

sources.title: Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Experiment 1: after five minutes restudying led (81% versus 75%); after one week testing led (56% versus 42%). Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Roediger and Karpicke (2006), Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention, Psychological Science 17(3), 249–255.

sources.title: ts-fsrs 5.4.1, the FSRS scheduler used by Discere
sources.licence: MIT licence (software); used for fact checking only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Stability is the interval at which predicted recall falls to 90%; the default requested retention is 0.9; version 5.4.1 defaults to the FSRS-6 decay of 0.1542. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Open Spaced Repetition contributors, ts-fsrs 5.4.1, the FSRS scheduler used by Discere, Package source, forgetting_curve and default parameters.

sources.title: A theory of Pavlovian conditioning
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Associative strength changes on each trial by a learning rate times the gap between the outcome's maximum and current strength. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Rescorla and Wagner (1972), A theory of Pavlovian conditioning, In Black and Prokasy (eds), Classical Conditioning II, 64–99.
sources.section: In Black and Prokasy (eds), Classical Conditioning II, 64–99

sources.title: Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: After a wheel stopped on 10 or 65, median estimates of the share of African countries in the UN were 25 and 45; base rates are neglected when individuating information is given. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases, Science 185(4157), 1124–1131.

sources.title: Measures of anchoring in estimation tasks
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Defines the anchoring index as the difference between high- and low-anchor median estimates divided by the difference between the anchors. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995), Measures of anchoring in estimation tasks, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 21(11), 1161–1166.

sources.title: Cognitive reflection and decision making
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: The cognitive reflection test uses problems whose fast intuitive answer is wrong, such as the bat-and-ball problem. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Frederick (2005), Cognitive reflection and decision making, Journal of Economic Perspectives 19(4), 25–42.

sources.title: Studies of independence and conformity: a minority of one against a unanimous majority
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Alone, judges erred on under 1% of line judgements; facing a unanimous wrong majority, about a third of critical answers conformed, about three quarters of people conformed at least once and about a quarter never did. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Asch (1956), Studies of independence and conformity: a minority of one against a unanimous majority, Psychological Monographs 70(9), 1–70.

sources.title: Behavioral study of obedience
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: 26 of 40 participants continued to the 450-volt switch. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Milgram (1963), Behavioral study of obedience, Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 67(4), 371–378.
sources.section: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 67(4), 371–378

sources.title: Replicating Milgram: would people still obey today?
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Stopping at 150 volts for ethical reasons, 70% of participants were willing to continue, against 82.5% in Milgram's comparable condition. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Burger (2009), Replicating Milgram: would people still obey today?, American Psychologist 64(1), 1–11.

sources.title: Behind the shock machine: the untold story of the notorious Milgram psychology experiments
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: Archival recordings show departures from the script and many participants who doubted the shocks were real. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Perry (2013), Behind the shock machine: the untold story of the notorious Milgram psychology experiments, The New Press, 2013.

sources.title: Bystander intervention in emergencies: diffusion of responsibility
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: 85% of participants who believed they alone heard a seizure helped before it ended, against 31% of those who believed four others heard it. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Darley and Latané (1968), Bystander intervention in emergencies: diffusion of responsibility, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 8(4), 377–383.
sources.section: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 8(4), 377–383

sources.title: The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping: the parable of the 38 witnesses
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: The story of 38 inactive witnesses is not supported by the trial evidence. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Manning, Levine and Collins (2007), The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping: the parable of the 38 witnesses, American Psychologist 62(6), 555–562.

sources.title: Would I be helped? Cross-national CCTV footage shows that intervention is the norm in public conflicts
sources.publisher: Philpot, Liebst, Levine, Bernasco and Lindegaard (2020)
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: In 219 recorded public conflicts in three cities, at least one bystander intervened in 91%, and more bystanders made intervention more likely. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Philpot, Liebst, Levine, Bernasco and Lindegaard (2020), Would I be helped? Cross-national CCTV footage shows that intervention is the norm in public conflicts, American Psychologist 75(1), 66–75.

sources.title: The bystander-effect: a meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies
sources.licence: All rights reserved by the publisher; reference only
sources.notes: Checked figure: The bystander effect is reliable on average but weaker in clearly dangerous emergencies. Discere states the figure in its own words; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Fischer and colleagues (2011), The bystander-effect: a meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies, Psychological Bulletin 137(4), 517–537.
